title: The Two Dragonflies
prompt: At first light two dragonflies rest together on the same lily, one swift and one slow, then lift off to circle the pond.
The swift one loops the whole pond once every minute. The slow one needs twelve minutes for a single loop. They fly the same way around, both starting from that shared lily.
Over the next twelve minutes, counting the moment they reunite on the starting lily, how many times do the two dragonflies meet?
hints: Ignore the pond and watch only the gap between them. The swift dragonfly pulls ahead of the slow one at a steady rate. How much of a loop does it gain each minute?
They meet every time the swift one has gained exactly one full loop on the slow one. So count loops gained, not minutes.
In twelve minutes the swift dragonfly flies twelve loops and the slow one flies a single loop, so the swift one gains eleven loops. Each gained loop is one meeting.
solution_lede:
The tempting answer is twelve, one meeting a minute, but that is not how circling works. The dragonflies only meet when the swift one has pulled a whole loop ahead of the slow one, and gaining a full loop takes a touch longer than a minute.

Watch the gap between them. The swift dragonfly gains at a rate of one loop minus one twelfth of a loop each minute, which is eleven twelfths of a loop every minute. A meeting happens each time that gap completes a whole loop. Over twelve minutes the swift one flies twelve loops while the slow one flies one, a gain of eleven loops in all. That is eleven meetings, the last arriving just as both settle back onto the lily.

solution_steps.body: The swift dragonfly gains on the slow one at eleven twelfths of a loop per minute.
They meet once for every whole loop the swift one gains, so meetings are counted by gained loops, not by minutes.
In twelve minutes the swift flies twelve loops and the slow flies one, a gain of eleven loops, so they meet eleven times.
